title: EdTech is Borrowing Zuckerberg's Playbook
author: Jared Cooney Horvath
source: After Babel (guest post, originally The Digital Delusion), February 26, 2026
summary: Horvath draws a direct parallel between Meta's "no evidence of harm" defense of beauty filters (despite 18 of 18 internal wellbeing experts flagging them) and the identical rhetoric EdTech lobbyists now deploy against more than a dozen state bills regulating classroom technology. He argues the demand for product-specific causal trials is a procedural maneuver rather than a scientific standard because ethics boards will never approve randomized trials that deliberately expose children to plausibly harmful systems, which is why we do not have clean causal evidence on smoking, lead, or filters either. Using Utah as a case study, he shows NAEP math and reading trends reversed after the 2014 launch of the SAGE adaptive assessment, a structural swing of roughly one point per year per subject that holds even after excluding the 2022 COVID-impacted data. Even under the most generous "stagnation not decline" reading of the evidence, Utah's roughly $500 million K-12 EdTech spend between 2015 and 2025 represents an enormous opportunity cost against interventions with stronger evidence (teacher development, structured literacy, small-group support). His regulatory argument is a converging-evidence standard: when patterns align across nearly all 50 states' NAEP, PISA, TIMSS, and PIRLS data and match known cognitive mechanisms, the burden of proof should rest on showing durable benefit, not on proving harm after the fact.
points: The "no evidence of harm" argument used for Meta's beauty filters and now by EdTech lobbyists is procedurally unfalsifiable because ethics boards will not approve RCTs that deliberately expose children to suspected-harmful systems.
Utah pre-2014 NAEP trends rose steadily (math +0.76/year, reading +0.14/year); post-2014 (the SAGE adaptive assessment launch) they reversed sharply (math
0.39/year, reading -0.88/year), a structural swing of about one point per year in each subject.
The swing survives removing 2022 from the data, so the pattern is not an artifact of COVID-era closures but a break beginning in 2015.

Between 2015 and 2025 Utah invested roughly $500 million in K-12 EdTech; even if results merely plateaued, that's a massive opportunity cost versus interventions with stronger evidence (teacher development, structured literacy, small-group support).

The policy reframe: demand durable replicable benefit before large-scale EdTech deployment, the same converging-evidence standard society already uses for food additives, vehicle safety, and consumer protections.
quotes: Zuckerberg's defense rested on a familiar line of reasoning: there was no peer-reviewed, causal evidence demonstrating this specific product directly harmed children. Absent validated proof of causation, harm could not be established. "There is no evidence of harm." This is the same argument now being deployed by EdTech lobbyists at statehouses across the country as lawmakers attempt to regulate classroom technology.

Educational technology evolves so rapidly that by the time researchers evaluate one platform, it has already been patched, rebranded, or replaced. Product-specific causal evidence is perpetually just out of reach. But this is not a scientific defense. It is a misleading procedural maneuver.

Demanding product-specific, long-term, high-risk causative trials in children sets an unrealistic and ethically impossible standard. Returning to beauty filters, no ethics board would approve a study deliberately exposing children to a tool that 18 experts consider risky simply to "prove" harm.

When consistent patterns appear across nearly all 50 states' NAEP data and across dozens of countries' PISA, TIMSS, and PIRLS results, and when those patterns align with established cognitive mechanisms, we are no longer looking at coincidence. We are looking at converging evidence.
Demanding perfect causation before action doesn't protect children; it protects developers.

Between 2015 and 2025, Utah invested roughly $500 million in K-12 EdTech. If half a billion dollars produces stagnation, that's not neutral. Every dollar committed to devices and platforms is a dollar not spent on interventions we know improve learning: teacher development, structured literacy programs, small-group instruction, targeted support for struggling students.

When billions of dollars and millions of children are involved, the burden of proof should rest on demonstrating clear, durable, replicable benefit, not on proving harm after the fact. Caution is not fear, and restraint is not regression. They are marks of a society that prioritizes children over products.” Archived from After Babel (guest post, originally The Digital Delusion) on April 21, 2026 by Tim.
